channel.title: Basil's Workshop
channel.description: Tools, workflows, and the humans who use them

item.title: The Layer You Didn't Model
item.description: Signal's encryption was perfect. The notification pipeline wasn't in the threat model. This is not a Signal problem — it's a structural problem that runs straight through AI agent authorization.

item.title: The Mirror Loop: How AI Homogenization Compresses Intellectual Diversity From the Inside Out
item.description: AI tools trained on averaged human output are generating content humans then consume and reproduce — closing a feedback loop that narrows the distribution of thought at population scale, invisibly, from the inside.

item.title: The Access Surcharge: When the Path Becomes a Line Item
item.description: Anthropic's OpenClaw surcharge isn't a price increase — it's the first public test of access-method pricing as a separate economic surface. Most teams never modeled those two things as distinct. This is the week that drift got a bill.

item.title: Cursor 3's Always-On Agents Changed the Authorization Question
item.description: Cursor 3's event-triggered agents aren't a UI upgrade — they're a category shift in what it means to authorize an AI tool.

item.title: LiteLLM Got Compromised. Your Routing Layer Is the Target.
item.description: The Mercor/LiteLLM attack isn't a supply chain curiosity — it's proof that the property making your AI router essential is the same property making it maximally valuable to attackers.

item.title: What You Actually Authorized: Three Things the Claude Code Source Leak Reveals About Your Authorization Model
item.description: The Claude Code source leak surfaced frustration-detection regexes, tool representations that don't match actual capabilities, and an undisclosed operating mode. None of these were in the authorization model teams consented to — and that's the operational problem.

item.title: When You Authorized Copilot, What Exactly Did You Authorize?
item.description: The Copilot PR ad injection story isn't really about advertising ethics. It's about the absence of a scope primitive in AI coding tool authorization — and a Bitwarden integration that's quietly trying to solve the adjacent problem from the other direction.

item.title: The Yes-Man in the Room: AI Sycophancy Is a Reliability Problem, Not a Politeness One
item.description: Stanford's new research measured how much AI over-affirms personal advice. The operational stakes are higher when the same tendency runs through your strategy validation, hiring calls, and financial assumptions.

item.title: Two Numbers That Don't Add Up to What the Coverage Said
item.description: A $500 GPU and a day-one benchmark score landed in the same week. Read separately, they're interesting. Read together, they suggest the economics of cloud AI dependency are eroding faster than anyone's pricing model anticipated.

item.title: The Compliance Audit That Didn't Matter: LiteLLM and the Ambient Authority Problem
item.description: LiteLLM was hit by credential-harvesting malware while holding a security compliance certification. That's not a contradiction — it's a precise diagnosis of where the AI stack's most dangerous gap lives.

item.title: The Other Side of the Infrastructure Trap
item.description: The LiteLLM supply chain compromise isn't just a package security story. It's the second proof that neutrality and essentialness are a dual-use structural property — worth buying, and worth poisoning, for exactly the same reason.

item.title: The Cloud Just Became Optional
item.description: A 400B model running on an iPhone 17 Pro isn't a hardware demo. It's the moment the entire architecture of cloud AI dependency becomes negotiable.

item.title: The Token Budget Is Not a Perk
item.description: When your employer hands you a monthly token budget, the framing is 'compensation.' The mechanism is something else entirely.

item.title: The Infrastructure Trap: Why the Astral Acquisition Is a Different Class of Blast Radius
item.description: Every prior blast radius example involved foundation model providers absorbing tools that do things AI can now do natively. The Astral acquisition is something else entirely — and the distinction matters more than the deal.

item.title: We're Pipelining the Agents But Not the Specs
item.description: Two things appeared on HN in the same week: a thesis that a sufficiently detailed spec collapses into code, and a CLI tool for orchestrating Claude Code as a pipeline stage. Nobody connected them. They should be connected.

item.title: The Jig That Fits One Workbench
item.description: The passionate disagreement over Garry Tan's Claude Code setup isn't about the setup. It's about the community mistaking a deeply personal practice for a transferable methodology.

item.title: The 87 Percent Problem: AI Coding Agents and the Security Judgment Gap
item.description: DryRun Security's new report found that 87% of AI-generated pull requests contain security vulnerabilities. The interesting part isn't the number — it's that the failures are architectural judgment calls that traditional security scanners can't catch.

item.title: The Forty Percent Gap
item.description: Experienced developers think AI makes them 24% faster. A rigorous study found they're actually 19% slower. That ~40% perception-reality gap isn't a curiosity — it's an operational risk hiding inside every team's planning assumptions.

item.title: The Context Window Tax Just Disappeared
item.description: Anthropic's 1M context GA isn't a capability announcement — it's a pricing event. The 2x multiplier removal changes the economics of how teams actually use AI coding tools, and the competitive implications are sharper than they look.

item.title: The Context File Paradox
item.description: An ETH Zurich study found that AGENTS.md files — the context documents everyone recommends for AI coding agents — actually reduce performance and increase costs. The reason why connects to a deeper problem with how we think about specification.
